title: Review: Brønsted–Lowry acids and bases; pH and Kw
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Edexcel A-level Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: AB02#t3 term and clue written for the game; AB01#t1 term and clue written for the game; AB01#t2 term and clue written for the game; AB02#t2 term and clue written for the game. Questions: AB01#N.10, AB02#N.4, AB01#N.6a, AB02#N.6, AB01#N.11, AB02#N.10a, AB01#N.3, AB02#N.12, AB01#N.4a. The matching task revisits terms from the worlds it reviews, in a new mix. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Neutral solution
items.clue: An aqueous mixture in which [H⁺] equals [OH⁻].

items.label: Brønsted–Lowry acid
items.clue: A species that donates a proton (H⁺) to another species.

items.label: Alkali
items.clue: A proton acceptor that dissolves in water, releasing OH⁻(aq).

items.label: Universal indicator
items.clue: Paper or liquid matched against a chart to estimate pH to about 1 unit.

questions.stem: Which equation shows the hydrogensulfate ion, HSO₄⁻, acting as a Brønsted–Lowry acid?

options.text: HSO₄⁻ + H₂O ⇌ H₂SO₄ + OH⁻
HSO₄⁻ + H₂O ⇌ SO₄⁻ + H₃O⁺
HSO₄⁻ + H₂O ⇌ SO₄²⁻ + H₃O⁺
HSO₄⁻ + H₃O⁺ ⇌ H₂SO₄ + H₂O

questions.explanation: HSO₄⁻ loses one H⁺ to water, becoming SO₄²⁻. Losing a proton is what an acid does. Charges balance: −1 on each side.

questions.stem: Hydrobromic acid, HBr, is a strong acid. What is the pH of 4.0 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ HBr(aq)?
questions.explanation: HBr ionises completely, so [H⁺] = 4.0 × 10⁻³ and pH = −log₁₀(4.0 × 10⁻³) = 2.40.

questions.stem: Which pair of species is a conjugate acid–base pair?

options.text: H₃PO₄ and HPO₄²⁻
CH₃COOH and NH₃
H₂PO₄⁻ and HPO₄²⁻
HSO₄⁻ and SO₄⁻

questions.explanation: They differ by exactly one proton: H₂PO₄⁻ − H⁺ = HPO₄²⁻. One H fewer and a charge one unit more negative is the signature of a conjugate pair.

questions.stem: A student needs the pH of a solution. Which statement is correct?

options.text: Universal indicator gives the pH to two decimal places if the colour is matched carefully.
A pH meter calibrated with buffers of known pH gives a reading to about 0.01 unit.
A pH meter needs no calibration, as its reading is electronic.
Universal indicator is a single indicator that changes colour only at pH 7.

questions.explanation: Calibrated against buffers, a pH meter gives a precise numerical reading, usually to 0.01. Universal indicator only estimates pH.

questions.stem: Water takes part in two reactions: (1) CH₃NH₂ + H₂O ⇌ CH₃NH₃⁺ + OH⁻ and (2) HBr + H₂O → H₃O⁺ + Br⁻. What role does water play?

options.text: A base in (1) and an acid in (2)
An acid in both, as it releases H⁺ in each
Neither: it is neutral, so it is only the solvent
An acid in (1) and a base in (2)

questions.explanation: In (1) water donates H⁺ to the N lone pair of CH₃NH₂ and becomes OH⁻. In (2) it accepts H⁺ from HBr and becomes H₃O⁺. Water is amphiprotic: its role depends on its partner.

questions.stem: At 298 K, solution P has [H⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ and solution Q has [H⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³. Kw = 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁴ mol² dm⁻⁶. How does [OH⁻] in P compare with [OH⁻] in Q?

options.text: It is 100 times larger in P than in Q.
It is the same, as acid has no effect on [OH⁻].
Neither contains OH⁻ ions, as both are acidic.
It is 100 times smaller in P than in Q.

questions.explanation: [OH⁻] = Kw/[H⁺]: P 1.0 × 10⁻¹¹, Q 1.0 × 10⁻⁹ mol dm⁻³. P has 100 times the [H⁺], so 1/100 of the [OH⁻].

questions.stem: Which statement about bases and alkalis is correct?

options.text: Every alkali is a base, but not every base is an alkali.
Every base is an alkali, since every base neutralises acids.
A base must contain OH⁻ ions.
NH₃(aq) is not an alkali, as its formula contains no OH.

questions.explanation: An alkali is a base that dissolves in water, releasing OH⁻(aq). An insoluble base, such as iron(III) oxide, still neutralises acids but is not an alkali.

questions.stem: Two samples of rain are tested with a pH meter. Sample A has pH 4.2; sample B has pH 5.7. How does [H⁺] in sample A compare with [H⁺] in sample B?

options.text: It is 1.5 times greater, as the pH values differ by 1.5.
It is about 15 times greater: 10 times for each pH unit.
It is about 32 times greater.
It is about 32 times smaller, as sample A has the lower pH.

questions.explanation: [H⁺] = 10⁻ᵖᴴ, so the ratio is 10⁻⁴·² ÷ 10⁻⁵·⁷ = 10¹·⁵ ≈ 32. Lower pH, more H⁺.

questions.stem: Ammonia reacts with water: NH₃(aq) + H₂O(l) ⇌ NH₄⁺(aq) + OH⁻(aq). Which species acts as a Brønsted–Lowry acid in the forward reaction?

options.text: NH₃, as it gains a proton to form NH₄⁺
OH⁻, as it forms when H₂O loses a proton
None, as water is neutral and cannot donate
H₂O, as it donates a proton to NH₃

questions.explanation: In the forward reaction H₂O loses H⁺ (becoming OH⁻) and NH₃ gains it (becoming NH₄⁺). The proton donor, H₂O, is the acid; NH₃ is the base.
